planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with reliable atmospheric humidity; Mexican Bigleaf Magnolia comes from montane cloud forest and is more cold-tender than its U.S. relative Bigleaf Magnolia (Magnolia macrophylla), so site it away from drying wind and hard freezes.

directions: Mexican Bigleaf Magnolia is a rare deciduous tree of the montane cloud forests of eastern Mexico — Veracruz, Puebla, Hidalgo, Oaxaca, and San Luis Potosi — where habitat loss has left it assessed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. It is closely related to, and sometimes classified as a subspecies of, the southeastern U.S. Bigleaf Magnolia (Magnolia macrophylla subsp. dealbata), but most horticultural and conservation references list it under its own name, distinguished by the whitened (dealbata means 'whitened') undersides of its enormous leaves. Its bowl-shaped white flowers can reach 16 inches or more across, among the largest of any magnolia, opening in late spring and followed by rose-pink, cone-like fruit clusters. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from wind and consistent humidity to protect the oversized leaves, and reserve it for warmer gardens (roughly zone 8 and up) since it lacks the cold hardiness of its Appalachian relatives.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Canary is a female selection and needs a male American holly such as Jersey Knight within about 50 feet for reliable fruit set.

directions: Canary is a female American holly selection notable for bright canary-yellow berries instead of the species' typical red, ripening in fall and holding well into winter against dark, spiny evergreen foliage. It grows into the same slow, sturdy pyramidal form as the species and makes a striking specimen or accent tree wherever a novelty holly color is wanted. Because it is female, fruiting depends on a nearby male American holly for pollination. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and give it room to develop into a substantial tree over time.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Morgan Gold American Holly (Gold-Fruited Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Morgan Gold is female and requires a nearby male American holly for cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Morgan Gold is a female American holly selection grown for its golden-yellow fall and winter fruit, offering an alternative to the more widely known yellow-berried cultivar Canary. It carries the species' typical dark, glossy, spiny leaves on a dense pyramidal frame and provides the same wildlife and winter-interest value as red-fruited hollies with a distinctive color twist. A male American holly must be sited nearby, since Morgan Gold sets little or no fruit without pollination. Grow in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the best foliage color and berry set.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Fallaw American Holly (Compact Yellow-Fruited Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fallaw is a female, compact selection and needs a male American holly nearby for its yellow berries to set.

directions: Fallaw is a female American holly selection valued for its compact, upright habit that stays noticeably smaller and denser than standard tree-form American hollies, while still producing yellow rather than red berries. Its tighter growth makes it useful where a full-size holly tree would outgrow the space, such as foundation plantings or narrow borders. Fruiting requires a nearby male American holly for pollination. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and expect slow, tidy growth into a dense, shrubby small tree.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: William Hawkins American Holly (Dwarf Male Pollinator Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; William Hawkins is a male-only dwarf selection grown as a compact pollen source, not for berries.

directions: William Hawkins is a dwarf male American holly that originated as a witches'-broom sport and is propagated by grafting, producing an unusually dense, low mound of narrow, linear leaves quite unlike the broad spiny foliage of typical American holly. As a male clone it never sets fruit, but its small stature makes it a practical compact pollen source for nearby female American hollies in gardens too small for a full-size male tree. It also stands on its own as a novelty dwarf conifer-like accent for rock gardens or foundation plantings. Grow in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Cardinal Hedge American Holly (Dwarf Hedging Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cardinal Hedge is female and needs a male American holly nearby for berry set, though it is grown chiefly as a dense low hedge.

directions: Cardinal Hedge is a dwarf female American holly selection that grows to only about four feet tall, far shorter than standard tree-form American hollies, while retaining the same dense, spiny dark-green foliage. Its naturally tidy, compact habit suits it to low clipped or informal hedges, foundation plantings, and borders where a full-size holly would be impractical. Given a male American holly nearby it can also carry a light crop of small red berries. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and shear lightly if a formal hedge line is wanted.

common_name: Cobalt American Holly (Cold-Hardy Male Pollinator Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cobalt is a male-only selection grown strictly as an especially cold-hardy pollen source for female American hollies.

directions: Cobalt is a male American holly selection distinguished by exceptional cold hardiness, reportedly tolerating temperatures down to about -32 degrees Celsius (roughly -26 Fahrenheit) — well beyond the cold tolerance typical of American holly and useful for extending reliable pollination into colder parts of the species' range. Like other male selections it never produces berries, but it grows into a dense, uniformly pyramidal evergreen useful as a screen or specimen tree in its own right. Site one within about 50 feet of several female American hollies for consistent fruit set. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yule is female and needs a male American holly nearby, such as Jersey Knight, for its heavy crop of large berries.

directions: Yule is a female American holly selection noted among named cultivars for its unusually large red berries, produced in heavy, showy clusters that hold well through the winter holiday season the cultivar's name evokes. It carries the species' classic dark, glossy, spiny leaves on a dense pyramidal frame and makes an excellent specimen or wildlife tree. Because it is female, a male American holly must be planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and the heaviest fruit set. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

common_name: Winter Snow American Holly (Variegated Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Winter Snow is female and needs a male American holly nearby for berry set.

directions: Winter Snow is a female American holly selection grown for its variegated foliage, each spiny dark-green leaf edged with a creamy-white margin that brightens the plant year-round and stands out against the plain green leaves of typical American holly. It grows into the same dense pyramidal form as the species, making an eye-catching specimen where foliage interest is wanted alongside the classic holly silhouette. As with other female selections, a male American holly must be planted nearby for the berries to set. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; variegated foliage colors best with some direct sun.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Butter Yellow Tea Olive (Compact Butter-Yellow Fragrant Osmanthus)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this compact selection blooms more heavily than seed-grown tea olive and fits foundation plantings where a smaller mature size is wanted.

directions: Butter Yellow is a slower-growing, denser tea olive selection prized for its soft, buttery-yellow flowers and heavier bloom set than typical seed-grown plants, with the same intensely sweet apricot fragrance that carries well beyond the shrub itself. Its tighter, more rounded habit suits smaller gardens, foundation plantings, and container culture better than the larger species form. Site it near an entry, patio, or window where the fragrance can be enjoyed during its main spring and fall bloom flushes. Water regularly during establishment, then expect good drought tolerance and only light shaping needed after flowering.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Nanjing Beauty Tea Olive (Vigorous Cold-Hardy Fragrant Osmanthus)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this vigorous Chinese selection is grown in part for its improved cold hardiness compared to typical seed-grown tea olive.

directions: Selected in Nanjing, China, this vigorous tea olive is grown for its fast, upright growth and notably better cold hardiness than typical seed-grown fragrans, allowing gardeners at the cooler edge of its range to grow it with more confidence. Clusters of small, intensely sweet, apricot-scented flowers appear in the heaviest flush during fall with lighter repeat bloom through the cooler months in mild climates. It forms a large, dense, upright shrub or small multi-trunk tree over time and takes well to hedging or occasional limbing up into a small specimen tree. Establish with regular water, then expect good tolerance of heat, humidity, and routine dry spells.
